opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes from having been burned, honestly, and from watching the field get burned a few times. In biology it's very easy to produce something that looks impressive on a benchmark or in a paper and then doesn't translate at all when it meets the real world. You can get a beautiful-looking structure prediction or a model that generates sequences with great in-silico metrics, and then you go to the wet lab and almost nothing works. The gap between "looks good computationally" and "actually does something useful in a cell or a patient" is enormous.

So for me the bar has to be: does this change what a scientist or a drug developer would actually do? If you're claiming you can design antibodies or binders with AI, then show me hit rates in the lab, against hard targets, not just the easy ones that have tons of data in the PDB. Show me it generalizes to things the model hasn't effectively memorized. A lot of the early excitement in the field came from tasks where the training and test data were closer together than people realized, and when you hold out properly the numbers drop a lot.

There's also the point that biology has a long history of hype cycles. Every decade there's a new technology that's going to revolutionize drug discovery, and people have become rightfully skeptical. If we want AI to be taken seriously by chemists, biologists, and pharma companies, we can't just say "trust us, the loss went down." We have to meet them on their terms, with experimental validation, with zero-shot results, with molecules that have properties that actually matter for therapeutics, not just binding but developability, specificity, all of it.

And frankly it keeps us honest internally. If you set a low bar, you'll clear it and convince yourself you're making progress when you're not. Setting a high bar means sometimes you look at the results and realize the approach doesn't work yet, and that's painful, but it's the only way you end up building something that's genuinely useful rather than something that just demos well.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between computational results and wet-lab usefulness, but does not say that small apparent improvements may be indistinguishable from wet-lab measurement variability.

r002.rationale: The response calls for generalization to hard or unseen targets, but does not argue that success on one or two tasks is insufficient to establish the broad applicability needed for a biological AI product.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that biology is unforgiving in a way most domains aren't. When a language model writes a slightly worse paragraph, you can read it and judge it in ten seconds. When a model proposes a protein, you don't know if it's any good until someone expresses it, purifies it, and runs an assay. That loop takes weeks and costs real money. So the cost of fooling yourself is enormous, and the field has a long history of doing exactly that.

Most of the self-deception comes from benchmarks. It's very easy to build a dataset where the model looks great because the test set leaks from the training set, or because the task is a proxy that doesn't correlate with anything a biologist actually cares about. You can get a beautiful curve on a held-out set of sequences and still have a model that produces nothing useful in a wet lab. I've seen that pattern enough times that I just don't trust in-silico numbers on their own anymore.

So the bar we set is: did something happen in the physical world that wouldn't have happened without the model? Did we make a molecule that binds, a cell that does what we asked, a therapeutic candidate that a drug hunter would actually want to carry forward? That's slow and expensive, but it's the only signal that can't be gamed.

There's also a cultural reason. Biologists are rightly skeptical. They've been promised that computation would transform their field for decades, and most of those promises didn't pan out. If we want them to actually adopt these tools, we have to show results that survive contact with reality, not demos. Overclaiming once sets the whole field back, because the next real result gets dismissed as hype too.

And frankly, the high bar is also what makes the work interesting. If we only measured things that were easy to measure, we'd end up optimizing for the wrong thing. Forcing ourselves to validate experimentally keeps the research honest about where the models actually are, and that's usually further behind the press releases but further ahead than the skeptics assume.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes the time and cost of wet-lab validation, but does not say that small apparent improvements can be obscured by measurement variability.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes proxy benchmarks and calls for real-world validation, but does not argue that success on one or two tasks is insufficient to establish the general applicability required for a product.

astra-6.text:
Because in biology, it’s really easy to get excited about a computational result that doesn’t translate into something useful in the lab. A model can do well on a benchmark, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s learned something that will help you design a better molecule or develop a better medicine.

So I think the bar has to be prospective experimental validation: can you make a prediction about something you haven’t tested, run the experiment, and show that it works? And can you do that consistently, against a meaningful baseline? Biology is complicated, and the feedback cycles are long. We want to know that we’re making progress on the underlying scientific problem, not just getting better at the benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark performance may not translate to lab usefulness, but it does not say small improvements may be indistinguishable from wet-lab measurement variability.

r002.rationale: The response calls for consistent results against a meaningful baseline, but does not argue that success on one or two tasks is insufficient to establish general applicability for a biological AI product.

sol-6.1.text: Because in biology, it’s very easy to build a model that looks impressive on a benchmark without showing that it can do something useful in the real world. The data are messy, and a model can pick up patterns that don’t generalize to a new experiment. So I want the evidence to connect the prediction to an actual biological result. Can you design something, make it, test it, and show that it works? That’s a much higher bar than getting a better score, but it’s the bar that matters if we want these models to help develop medicines.
